content: 1. Drotrecogin-α (Xigris®) is primarily utilized for the treatment of severe sepsis. 2. This medication is a recombinant form of human activated protein C, which exhibits antithrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and profibrinolytic properties. 3. Tickborne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a bacterial illness caused by specific Borrelia species and transmitted through brief, painless bites from Ornithodoros ticks. 4. The disease is typically characterized by intermittent episodes of fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. 5. In April 2005, the CDC received reports of two cases of severe TBRF associated with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in residents of California and Nevada. 6. Following the publication of these cases on the CDC's Epidemic Information Exchange (Epi-X), health officials in Washington reported a third severe case associated with ARDS. 7. This report summarizes the three cases and the findings of subsequent epidemiologic investigations. 8. The findings suggest that ARDS may occur more frequently in patients with TBRF than previously recognized. 9. Optimal management of TBRF requires prompt diagnosis and careful monitoring during the initial phases of treatment. 10. On February 17, 2005, a previously healthy 46-year-old woman from Washoe County, Nevada, developed nonspecific leg pain, which progressed to generalized myalgia within 24 hours. 11. She visited a local hospital emergency department (ED), where she was diagnosed with a viral syndrome. 12. She was treated with intravenous (IV) fluids and pain medication and discharged home. 13. Two days later, she returned to the ED with fever, chills, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, and a syncopal episode. 14. 89 mm Hg) with a temperature of 96.8°F (36.0°C). 15. A physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. 16. Pulse oximetry on room air indicated an oxygen saturation of 96%. 17. Initial laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 11.4 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin level of 13 g/dL, platelet count of 66 × 10³/µL, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 153 U/L. 18. A chest radiograph showed a right middle lobe infiltrate consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. 19. She was treated with gatifloxacin and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). 20. Approximately 10 hours after admission, she was intubated for worsening tachypnea (respiratory rate: 40 breaths per minute). 21. Diffuse bilateral infiltrates were noted on a chest radiograph, and an arterial blood gas sample showed oxygenation of 53 mm Hg on 100% inspired oxygen. 22. The patient’s antimicrobial treatment was expanded to include vancomycin and doxycycline. 23. The following day, the treating physician was informed that spirochetes were observed during the examination of a blood smear obtained at admission; the smear had been manually reviewed due to thrombocytopenia. 24. The patient remained intubated for 12 days for what was ultimately determined to be ARDS. 25. During this time, she received three additional antimicrobials (ciprofloxacin, tobramycin, and ceftriaxone) and drotrecogin-α. 26. She was discharged after 21 days and made a full recovery. 27. The causative organism was identified as Borrelia hermsii through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) performed on a whole blood sample and serologic testing of convalescent-phase serum, both conducted at the CDC. 28. Although the patient did not recall a tick bite, she reported staying at a resort near South Lake Tahoe, an area highly endemic for TBRF, five days before becoming ill. 29. On April 12, 2005, a previously healthy 43-year-old woman from El Dorado County, California, developed lethargy and myalgia. 30. She visited a local hospital ED on April 14 with fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and dehydration. 31. She was febrile (100. 97 mm Hg). 32. A physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. 33. Pulse oximetry on room air indicated an oxygen saturation of 97%. 34. A chest radiograph was not obtained, but initial blood tests showed an elevated bilirubin level of 3.6 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 93 U/L, and ALT of 88 U/L. 35. She was treated with acetaminophen and discharged home with instructions to return for reevaluation of blood tests the next day. 36. The patient returned the next day with headache, sweating, fatigue, and nausea. 37. A physical examination revealed rhonchi; a chest radiograph was obtained and interpreted as normal. 38. She was treated with IV fluids and IV ceftriaxone. 39. 40. TBRF was diagnosed by observing spirochetes in smears of peripheral blood. 41. The patient was treated with dopamine for hypotension and doxycycline for TBRF and transferred to another medical center. 42. Shortly after arrival, a chest radiograph taken due to worsening respiratory distress demonstrated diffuse bilateral infiltrates. 43. The patient was intubated for respiratory failure (respiratory rate: 44 breaths per minute; oxygen saturation of 82% on 100% inspired oxygen via nonrebreather mask) attributed to ARDS. 44. Laboratory testing revealed a WBC of 3.4 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin level of 11.4 g/dL, and platelet count of 19 × 10³/µL. 45. Platelets and fresh frozen plasma were administered. 46. The patient remained intubated for 10 days, during which she received four different antimicrobials (vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, metronidazole, and doxycycline) and drotrecogin-α. 47. She was discharged after 19 days of hospitalization and eventually recovered from her illness. 48. A blood sample obtained early in her illness and cultured at the CDC yielded Borrelia hermsii. 49. An environmental investigation at her home, located five miles south of Lake Tahoe and approximately 10 miles from the resort visited by the Nevada patient, revealed an engorged soft tick in her bedroom and multiple rodent nests containing approximately 30 Ornithodoros hermsi ticks. 50. A 40-year-old woman from King County, Washington, visited a hospital ED on September 21, 2004, with myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, vomiting, and headache. 51. She was treated with IV fluids, promethazine, and hydrocodone. 52. Hospital admission was recommended, but she refused. 53. 100 mm Hg), mildly tachycardic (107 bpm), and hypoxic (oxygen saturation: 92% on 4 L of oxygen). 54. A physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. 55. Her chest radiograph revealed bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. 56. Initial laboratory studies indicated a WBC of 9.5 × 10³/µL, hematocrit of 33%, platelet count of 49 × 10³/µL, ALT of 192 U/L, and a D-dimer of 754. 57. She was admitted for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis and treated empirically with IV cefuroxime and azithromycin. 58. After receiving cefuroxime, she became transiently hypotensive and somnolent. 59. She was intubated and transferred to the ICU with a diagnosis of ARDS and worsening mental status. 60. A peripheral blood smear was examined due to thrombocytopenia, revealing spirochetes diagnostic of TBRF. 61. Her transient hypotension was attributed to a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR). 62. She remained intubated for three days, was discharged home after 10 days, and eventually recovered from her illness. 63. 64. Inspection of the cabin revealed evidence of rodent infestation; however, attempts to trap ticks and rodents were unsuccessful.
